format: personal experience interview, live Python coding exercise, 60 minutes
shape_name: A personal experience interview and a technical interview in one sitting

parts.title: Hello, and tell me about yourself

say.t: Thanks for making the time, I've been looking forward to talking about the planning work at Fernhill Freight.
I'm an operations analyst with seven years turning warehouse, transport and supplier data into forecasts and decisions that move stock and vans, most recently at Brindle & Hart Logistics.

The work I'm proudest of is a weekly [[demand-forecast|demand forecast]] I rebuilt there, which took [[forecast-error|forecast error]] from 22% to 14%, and it is the story I'd most like to walk you through today.

parts.bridge: So that is the short version, and I'm happy to start wherever is most useful to you.

parts.title: One story in depth, and the probes behind it

say.t: The story I'd like to tell in depth is the forecast I rebuilt at Brindle & Hart Logistics, because it shows how I work from a messy problem through to a result the planners trusted.

Trust is usually the first thing people ask about with a forecast, so I'll take it head on: I showed the planners the error by distribution centre every week, so they could see for themselves where it held and where it did not.
It was not all smooth, and the part I learned most from was getting 30+ operations managers to agree one definition of [[service-level|service level]], which I can go into as well.

parts.bridge: That is the outline, and I can go deeper on any part of it.

parts.title: A problem, worked aloud

say.t: Before I write anything I'll say back what I think the problem is and ask what the data looks like, so that we agree on the inputs and the output.
Then I'll talk through a plain first version in Python, test it on a small example I can check by hand, and only then tidy it or make it faster.
If I get stuck I'll say what I'm thinking rather than go quiet, and the way I like to work is the way I rebuilt a warehouse feed as [[dbt]] models, in small steps with a test on each.

parts.bridge: That is how I'd like to work through it, if that suits you.

steps.say: Can I say it back and check what the data looks like first?
I'll take the error as the gap over actual demand, as a share.
I'll loop over each SKU and skip any with no actual demand.
Let me run a few rows I can work out myself, to check it.
Now it's right, I'd move it into pandas if the data is large.

stuck: Can I talk through what I'm thinking for a second?
Let me write the simplest version first, then improve it.
edges: No actual demand in a week
The same SKU and week twice
Forecast rows with no actual to match

code.means: The gap as a share of actual demand
Skip a week with no demand, never divide by nothing
The same sum over a whole column at once
Each SKU over the threshold, once

more: With more time I'd add tests for the awkward weeks.
With more time I'd weight the error by how much each SKU sells.

say.t: When you push on my solution I'll take each trade-off out loud, what it costs in speed or in how easy it is to read, and what I'd choose for a weekly job.
Where I don't know something I'll say so and reason from what I do know, rather than guess.
I'd like to use the last few minutes on the work itself, starting with the Warrington [[cross-dock]] and what it has changed for the planning team.
Before we finish I'll ask whether there is anything in my background you'd like me to go into more, so that no doubt is left unanswered.

questions.q: Tell me about your experience with demand forecasting.
also: How have you forecast demand before?
questions.simple: Forecasting is the centre of my work, and the clearest example is at Brindle & Hart Logistics. I rebuilt the weekly demand forecast in Python and SQL, with promotions and seasonality as features, and forecast error came down from 22% to 14% across 2,400 SKUs. That let the planners release about £1.1M of safety stock they had been holding to cover the gap.
questions.detailed: Forecasting is the centre of my work, and the clearest example is at Brindle & Hart Logistics. Forecast error sat at 22% across 2,400 SKUs and six distribution centres, and the planners were covering the gap with extra safety stock. I rebuilt the weekly forecast in Python and SQL, with promotions and seasonality as features, and tracked the error by distribution centre so the planners could see where it held. Error came down to 14%, about £1.1M of safety stock was released, and I learned that a forecast only counts once its users can check it themselves.
from: What the letter answered it with: Cut forecast error from 22% to 14% across 2,400 SKUs at Brindle & Hart Logistics
Your story: The forecast that freed safety stock (it carries the letter's evidence)

follow.q: What was your part in it, exactly?
follow.simple: I built the model and the weekly error tracking myself, from the raw data through to the numbers the planners saw. The planners owned the stock decisions it fed, and I worked with them each week on where the forecast held.

follow.q: What didn't work?
follow.simple: The first version leaned too hard on last year's sales, and it missed the promotions badly. Once promotions went in as an input of their own, the error came down to where the planners could use it.

follow.q: How did you know it had worked?
follow.simple: I tracked the error by distribution centre every week against what actually sold, so it was measured rather than felt. It came down from 22% to 14%, and the planners released about £1.1M of safety stock on the strength of it.

follow.q: And where did it not hold?
follow.simple: It held least on new lines with little history, where there was not much for the model to learn from. I showed those to the planners as they were, so they kept their own judgement on those lines and used the forecast on the rest.

follow.q: Who disagreed, and how did you handle it?
follow.simple: Some planners doubted it at first, because the old figures were the ones they knew. I showed them the error by distribution centre each week, so they could judge it for themselves.

follow.q: What would you do differently now?
follow.simple: I would bring the planners in earlier, at the point of choosing the features, because they knew which promotions mattered long before the data showed it. I would also publish the error by site from the first week, since that was what won their trust.

questions.q: What is your experience with SAP?
also: How well do you know SAP?
questions.simple: My experience with SAP is on the reporting side, where I have reported from SAP extracts and the warehouse system behind them. I have not configured it or worked inside it as a planner would, and I would rather say that plainly. What I can do from the first week is turn what it holds into a forecast, in Python and SQL.
questions.detailed: My experience with SAP is on the reporting side, where I have reported from SAP extracts and the warehouse system behind them. I have not configured it or worked inside it as a planner would, and I would rather say that plainly than have you find out later. What I can do from the first week is turn what it holds into a forecast in Python and SQL, as I did for the weekly forecast across 2,400 SKUs at Brindle & Hart Logistics. I'd expect to learn your own set-up quickly from someone who knows it well.
from: I have reported from SAP extracts and the warehouse system behind them.
What the letter answered it with: Reported from SAP extracts and the warehouse system behind them

questions.q: Are you a member of CIPS?
also: Do you hold a procurement qualification?
questions.simple: No, I'm not a member of CIPS, and I'd rather say that plainly. My route into planning has been through the data, seven years of forecasting, stock and service-level work, rather than through procurement. If membership matters for this role, I'd like to understand what it is needed for.
questions.detailed: No, I'm not a member of CIPS, and I'd rather say that plainly. My route into planning has been through the data, rather than through procurement. Where I have worked closest to it is with the buyers at Oakmere Foods, whose order changes cut write-offs 18% over two quarters. If membership matters for this role, I'd like to understand what it is needed for.

questions.q: Walk me through some code you're proud of.
also: Show me something you have built.
questions.simple: The code I'm proudest of is the warehouse feed I rebuilt as dbt models with data-quality tests. Before it, someone spent two hours every morning reconciling the feed against the reports, and afterwards a bad load failed loudly instead of surfacing in a report. It is plain, well-tested code, which is what I'd aim for today as well.
questions.detailed: The code I'm proudest of is the warehouse feed I rebuilt as dbt models with data-quality tests. Before it, someone spent two hours every morning reconciling the feed against the reports built on it. I split the feed into small models, each doing one thing, and put a test on every assumption the reports relied on, so a bad load failed loudly instead of surfacing in a report. The reconciliation ended, and it is plain, well-tested code, which is what I'd aim for today as well.

questions.q: Tell me about a hard bug you tracked down.
questions.simple: The hardest was a forecast that looked right in total and wrong by site. It took me a while to see that two distribution centres were counted under one code after a system change. I found it by checking the inputs site by site against the warehouse records, rather than staring at the model. Since then I test the joins before I trust any number built on them.
questions.detailed: The hardest was a forecast that looked right in total and wrong by site, and it took me a while to see that two distribution centres were being counted under one code after a system change. I had spent a day looking at the model before I thought to doubt the data going into it. I found it by checking the inputs site by site against the warehouse records, and the fix was a test that every site appears once and only once. Since then I test the joins before I trust any number built on them.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you changed someone's mind.
also: How do you handle conflicting numbers?
Tell me about getting people to adopt your work.
questions.simple: I had 30+ operations managers reading service levels from eleven spreadsheets, and the numbers disagreed. I built one Power BI report, agreed the definitions with the managers team by team, and retired each spreadsheet as its team moved over. Nobody was told to switch, they moved because the one report answered their questions.
questions.detailed: I had 30+ operations managers reading service levels from eleven spreadsheets, and the numbers disagreed. I built one Power BI report and agreed the definition of service level with the managers team by team, before I showed anyone a chart. I retired each spreadsheet as its team moved over, and nobody was told to switch, they moved because the one report answered their questions. It taught me that people change their minds about numbers once they have had a hand in defining them.
from: Your story: One report in place of eleven spreadsheets (matched by its Use for tags)

follow.q: What was your part in it, exactly?
follow.simple: I built the report and ran the conversations about the definitions myself. The managers decided when their own team was ready to give up its spreadsheet, which is why the change held.

follow.q: What didn't work?
follow.simple: My first try was to build the report and show it, and nobody moved over. It only worked once the managers had agreed the definitions with me, team by team.

follow.q: How did you know it had worked?
follow.simple: I knew it had worked when the last of the eleven spreadsheets was retired and the 30+ managers were all reading the one report. The arguments about whose number was right stopped, because there was only one number.

follow.q: Who disagreed, and how did you handle it?
follow.simple: A couple of managers argued their own spreadsheet was the right one, and they had a point about how late orders were counted. I took their rule into the shared definition, and they moved over after that.

follow.q: What would you do differently now?
follow.simple: I would agree the definitions before building anything at all, since that was the slow part and the part that mattered. The report itself was the easy half.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you took something on without being asked.
also: Tell me about a process you improved.
questions.simple: Every morning someone spent two hours reconciling the warehouse data feed against the reports built on it, and nobody had asked me to fix it. I rebuilt the feed as dbt models with data-quality tests, so a bad load failed loudly instead of surfacing in a report. The daily two-hour reconciliation ended.
questions.detailed: Every morning someone spent two hours reconciling the warehouse data feed against the reports built on it, and nobody had asked me to fix it. I thought the manual step should go rather than be absorbed for ever, so I rebuilt the feed as dbt models with data-quality tests. From then on a bad load failed loudly at the start of the day instead of surfacing in a report at the end of it. The daily two-hour reconciliation ended.
from: Your story: Ending a daily reconciliation (matched by its Use for tags)

follow.q: Why did nobody ask you to fix it?
follow.simple: Because it had become part of the morning, and people had stopped seeing it as a problem. I only noticed because I was the one waiting for the reports it held up.

follow.q: What did the tests check?
follow.simple: They checked that each load was complete and that the values made sense before anything was built on it, for example that no site came through blank. A failed test stopped the run, so nobody read a report built on a bad load.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you worked with someone very different from you.
also: Tell me about working with a commercial team.
questions.simple: At Oakmere Foods I worked with the buyers for the chilled lines, who think in orders and suppliers where I think in data. Chilled stock was being lost to expiry, so I modelled shelf life against order patterns and gave them specific order changes rather than a general finding. Write-offs fell 18% over two quarters.
questions.detailed: At Oakmere Foods I worked with the buyers for the chilled lines, who think in orders and suppliers where I think in data. Chilled stock was being lost to expiry, and ordering took no account of shelf life, so I modelled how the two interact for those lines. I gave the buyers specific order changes they could make that week, rather than a general finding. Write-offs fell 18% over two quarters, and I learned to hand people a decision in their own terms, not an analysis in mine.
from: Your story: Chilled-line write-offs (matched by its Use for tags)

follow.q: What was your part in it, exactly?
follow.simple: The modelling was mine, and so was turning it into order changes the buyers could act on. The buyers made the changes with their suppliers, which only they could do.

follow.q: How did you know it had worked?
follow.simple: Write-offs on the chilled lines fell 18% over two quarters, measured against the same lines before the change. The buyers kept the new order patterns, which told me as much as the number did.

follow.q: What would you do differently now?
follow.simple: I would sit with the buyers for a day before modelling anything, to learn how they place an order. I worked some of that out the slow way, from the data.

questions.q: Tell me about something you owned that went wrong.
also: Tell me about a mistake you made.
questions.simple: An early version of my weekly forecast went out with a promotion missing from its inputs, and one distribution centre ran short that week. I told the planners the same day, and I added a check that every planned promotion was in the data before the forecast ran. It did not happen again, and I now test the inputs as carefully as the model.
questions.detailed: An early version of my weekly forecast went out with a promotion missing from its inputs, and one distribution centre ran short that week. I told the planners the same day rather than wait for them to find it, and we covered the gap from a neighbouring site. Then I added a check that every planned promotion was in the data before the forecast ran, so the same mistake could not get through twice. It did not happen again, and I now test the inputs as carefully as the model.

questions.q: What are the trade-offs in your approach?
also: Why did you write it that way?
questions.simple: The plain loop is the easiest to read and to check, and it is slower than working on whole columns. For a weekly job that matters very little, so I'd keep it readable. I'd change my mind if the same code had to run across every SKU every hour.
questions.detailed: The plain loop is the easiest to read and to check, and it is slower than working on whole columns. For a weekly job that matters very little, so I'd keep it readable and spend the time on tests instead. Working on whole columns is faster and shorter, and harder to step through when a number looks wrong. I'd change my mind if the same code had to run across every SKU every hour.

questions.q: Given weekly demand and forecasts by SKU, write a function that returns the SKUs whose forecast error is above a threshold.
also: Flag the lines where the forecast was furthest out.
simple: Return SKUs with forecast error over threshold
Say it back: error as share of actual
Ask: missing weeks, share or units
Plain loop first, skip zero demand
Small hand-worked tests, so the flags are trusted
questions.detailed: So I'd return every [[sku|SKU]] whose forecast error is over the threshold. First I'll say it back, to check we agree. The error is the gap between forecast and actual, as a share of actual. Before I type, I'd ask what the data looks like. Can a SKU miss a week? Is the threshold a share or a number of units? Then I'll write it plainly, as a loop that skips any SKU with no actual demand, so I never divide by zero. Once that's right, I'll ask how big the data is, and if it's large I'd move it into pandas. And I'd want a few small tests I can work out by hand, so we both trust what it flags.

follow.q: How would you test it?
simple: Under, over and on the threshold
Zero actual demand, where it breaks
follow.detailed: I'd test it on a few cases I can work out by hand. One SKU well under the threshold, one well over, and one right on it. Then the awkward one, a SKU with zero actual demand, because that's where it'd break.

follow.q: What if actual demand is zero?
simple: Zero demand: the share means nothing
Leave it out of the percentage
List apart for planners to see
follow.detailed: If actual demand is zero, the error as a share has no meaning. So I'd leave that SKU out of the percentage, but I wouldn't drop it altogether. I'd list it apart, because a planner may still want to see those lines.

follow.q: Would planners still want to see those lines?
simple: No sales can still mean stock tied up
follow.detailed: Yes, planners would still want those lines. A line with no sales can still have stock sitting on it, and that's money tied up. So I'd show them in their own short list, for the planners to judge.

follow.q: Can you make it faster?
simple: Faster with pandas, whole columns at once
Plain loop does for thousands of SKUs
follow.detailed: Yes, it can be faster. The plain loop is fine for a few thousand SKUs. For more than that, I'd move it into pandas, so the sums run over whole columns at once. But only once the simple version's right, because a fast wrong answer helps nobody.

questions.q: What would you do differently with more time?
questions.simple: I'd add tests for the awkward inputs first, missing weeks, negative returns and SKUs that changed code, since those are what break a forecast in practice. Then I'd move the threshold out of the code and into a setting, so a planner could change it without me.
questions.detailed: I'd add tests for the awkward inputs first, missing weeks, negative returns and SKUs that changed code, since those are what break a forecast in practice. Then I'd move the threshold out of the code and into a setting, so a planner could change it without me, and I'd write down what the function assumes about its inputs so the next person need not guess.

questions.q: How do you get depot managers to trust a forecast?
also: Why would a site manager believe your numbers?
questions.simple: I show them the evidence rather than ask for their trust. At Brindle & Hart Logistics I tracked forecast error by distribution centre every week. Each planner could see where the forecast held for their own site, and where it did not. Once they could check it for themselves they used it, and the safety stock came down.
questions.detailed: I show them the evidence rather than ask for their trust. At Brindle & Hart Logistics I tracked forecast error by distribution centre every week, so each planner could see where the forecast held for their own site and where it did not. I never argued for the model in a meeting, I put the weekly error in front of the people who would live with it. Once they could check it for themselves they used it, error came down from 22% to 14%, and about £1.1M of safety stock was released.

demand-forecast.name: Demand forecast
demand-forecast.here: At Fernhill Freight, the weekly estimate of how many pallets each [[cross-dock]] site will move, which is the forecast this role owns.
demand-forecast.example: If the Warrington site moved 1,000 pallets last week and a customer's promotion starts on Monday, the forecast for next week might be 1,150.
demand-forecast.plain: A best estimate of how much will be needed, made from what happened before.
demand-forecast.technical: A time-series model of volume by site and week.
demand-forecast.like: Like guessing how many people will come to a party from how many came last year, and who said yes.

forecast-error.name: Forecast error
forecast-error.here: At Fernhill Freight, how far the pallets a site was forecast to move were from the pallets it actually moved, as a share of the actual.
forecast-error.example: If Warrington was forecast 1,100 pallets and moved 1,000, the error for that week is 10%.
forecast-error.plain: The gap between what was predicted and what happened.
forecast-error.technical: Usually measured as mean absolute percentage error, by site and week.
forecast-error.like: Like a weather forecast that said ten millimetres of rain when five fell: the size of the miss.

cross-dock.name: Cross-dock
cross-dock.here: A Fernhill Freight site where pallets come off one lorry and go straight onto another, with little or no storage in between. Fernhill runs fourteen of them across the North of England.
cross-dock.example: Forty pallets arrive at Warrington at six, and by eight they are on three outbound lorries.
cross-dock.plain: A depot that moves goods straight through instead of storing them.
cross-dock.like: Like a sorting room in a post office: parcels come in one door and leave by another the same morning.

safety-stock.name: Safety stock
safety-stock.here: At Fernhill Freight, the spare room a site keeps in case the [[demand-forecast|forecast]] is wrong, which a better forecast lets the planners reduce.
safety-stock.example: If Warrington expects 1,000 pallets and plans for 1,150 to be safe, the extra 150 is the safety margin.
safety-stock.plain: Extra stock or room kept in case demand is higher than expected.
safety-stock.technical: Sized from forecast error and the service level wanted.
safety-stock.like: Like keeping a spare loaf in the freezer in case guests turn up.

sku.name: SKU
sku.here: One distinct product line in a Fernhill Freight customer's range, counted on its own when demand is forecast.
sku.example: A customer's small and large bottles of the same drink are two SKUs, each with its own forecast at Fernhill.
sku.plain: A single product, as a stock system counts it.
sku.like: Like each size and colour of a shoe having its own barcode in a shop.

dbt.name: dbt
dbt.here: A tool for building tested data tables in SQL, which at Fernhill Freight could turn the raw feed from each cross-dock into the tables a forecast reads.
dbt.example: A dbt test stops the load if Warrington's pallets for a day come through blank, before any Fernhill report uses them.
dbt.plain: A way of writing the steps that clean data as code, with checks built in.
dbt.technical: SQL models with schema and data tests, run in dependency order.
dbt.like: Like a recipe card for tidying the data, with a taste test after every step.

service-level.name: Service level
service-level.here: At Fernhill Freight, the share of pallets delivered on time and in full to the customer.
service-level.example: If 970 of 1,000 pallets leave Warrington on time and in full, the service level is 97%.
service-level.plain: How often the customer gets what was promised, when it was promised.
service-level.like: Like a pizza shop's promise to deliver within half an hour, and how often it keeps it.

feature.name: Feature
feature.plain: One piece of information a model learns from, such as the week of the year.
feature.here: At Fernhill Freight, what the pallet forecast would learn from: promotions, bank holidays and the season.
feature.like: Like the clues a detective weighs: each says little alone, and together they point to an answer.
feature.technical: An input column to the model.

sql.name: SQL
sql.plain: The language used to ask a database for exactly the rows you want.
sql.here: At Fernhill Freight, how you'd pull each site's weekly pallets and forecasts out of their systems.
sql.like: Like asking a librarian for every book by one author from one year, and getting just those.

sap.name: SAP
sap.plain: A large business system many firms use to run orders, stock and accounts in one place.
sap.here: At Fernhill Freight, it may be where each site's orders and stock are recorded, which a forecast would read from.
sap.like: Like the main ledger of a shop that every till and stockroom writes into.

cips.name: CIPS
cips.plain: The professional body for people who work in buying and supply.
cips.here: At Fernhill Freight, a membership some buying roles ask for; this role is about forecasting instead.
cips.like: Like a trade body for plumbers: membership shows you've met its standards.

join.name: Join
join.plain: Lining up two tables row by row on something they share, such as a product code.
join.here: At Fernhill Freight, lining up each week's forecast with what each site actually moved, before the error is worked out.
join.like: Like matching each guest on a list to their name badge before handing them out.

power-bi.name: Power BI
power-bi.plain: A program for building charts and reports that update themselves from the data.
power-bi.here: At Fernhill Freight, the kind of report planners and site managers could read the forecast in.
power-bi.like: Like a car's dials: the numbers you need, in one place, kept current.

known.text: How do you get depot managers to trust a forecast?
known.question: q15

private.pay: say what the form said, GBP 48,000 to 58,000: a recruiter checks what you say against it
not_to_say: Do not call it a parcel carrier: it moves pallets.
figures: Your lowest figure, 42,000: it stays with you.

weaknesses.frame: Say: “I have reported from SAP extracts and the warehouse system behind them.”
You do not hold it, so never claim it. Say so plainly, then the nearest true thing.

red_flags: Speaking badly of an employer you have worked for.
A number your own work does not hold, or one you cannot explain if asked how.
Naming the other employers you are talking to, or an offer you do not have.
"I'll take anything": say why this role, every time.
Answering a question they did not ask: answer, then stop.
